title: Slot lemma as a van der Blij / Gauss–Milgram formula for odd lattices (characteristic covectors)
connection: For an odd lattice, the Gauss sum of the discriminant form is governed by σ − w² mod 8, where w is a characteristic covector (van der Blij, Brown invariant). For the chain lattice, w has coordinates (v,t,u) mod 2 and w² has denominator p. This plausibly yields (A/p) as a function of p mod 8 and the parity pattern of (t,u,v,tu−1,tv−1), i.e. the slot lemma.
why: It would give the slot lemma a structural (lattice-theoretic) proof and a generalisation to chains of any length, i.e. an exact sign rule for λ(p) ≤ L words.
first_step: Compute σ − w² mod 8 symbolically for the 3-chain and compare with the slot-lemma indicator over all parity classes of (t,u,v) mod 8; then do the 4-chain.
refs: van der Blij, An invariant of quadratic forms mod 8 (1959)

title: Transport laws as a semigroup action: ES failures form a set closed under 'inverse transport'
connection: ES(m) ⇒ ES(km) trivially, and the repo has transport laws between different n. The failure set F is downward-closed under divisibility (if ES(n) fails then ES(d) fails for all d | n). Order theory: F is an order ideal in (ℕ, |).
why: Order-ideal structure plus density-zero (Vaughan) gives constraints, e.g. F ∩ primes determines F. Translating richer transport laws into a semigroup acting on ℕ gives an algebraic object (orbit closures).
first_step: List all proved transport laws (TRANSPORT_LAW.md, DELTA_TRANSPORT.md) as maps n ↦ f(n). Compute the semigroup they generate and its orbits on primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Mod-p relaxation: depth-3 products in SL₂(F_p) generated by M(b) and Helfgott growth
connection: Modulo p, tuv − u − v ≡ 0 allows words of kp for any k. In SL₂(F_p), the set X = {M(b) : b ∈ F_p} grows: X·X·X is large (Helfgott, Bourgain–Gamburd). This is the mod-p relaxation of ES₅ (losing the archimedean size condition).
why: It isolates the archimedean condition (tuv − u − v = p exactly) as the whole content, a sharp calibration: the algebraic mod-p problem is easy, and the size cut is hard.
first_step: Record the mod-p statement: for each p, does M(v)M(t)M(u) ≡ upper-triangular-with-sign have solutions with t,u,v small? Find the smallest letter bound needed vs p.
refs: Helfgott, Growth and generation in SL₂(ℤ/pℤ) (Ann. Math. 2008)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Eisenstein's lattice-point proof of reciprocity applied to Σ_{words} (A/p)
connection: Eisenstein proves reciprocity by counting lattice points under a line. The sign of a word reduces by reciprocity to (−t/A)-type symbols, and Gauss's lemma turns these into lattice-point parities. Summing over words gives a lattice-point count in a region bounded by hyperbolas and lines.
why: A lattice-point expression for N₊ − N₋ would make the sign sum a geometry-of-numbers object with possible exact evaluation.
first_step: Write (A/p) for A = tu − 1 via Gauss's lemma as (−1)^{#lattice points}; sum over words for small p and look for a region whose lattice-point count equals N₊ − N₋.

title: Ehrhart theory for the word region: quasi-polynomial in p for fixed letters
connection: For a fixed letter t, the number of words of level t as a function of p is a divisor-type count, not a quasi-polynomial. Restricted to fixed (t,u), it is a periodic function of p (Ehrhart in 1D).
why: It explains exactly where the Ehrhart (polynomial) structure breaks: at the hyperbola. Native calibration.
first_step: Calibration only: write the counts and note the hyperbolic break.

title: Unifying lemma across fields: pairing class = slot-lemma sign = lens homotopy class = K-matrix anyon class
connection: For a word (t,u,v), the following should be the same bit: (A/p); the sandpile pairing class of the fan; Whitehead's homotopy class of L(p,A); the discriminant-form class of the chain lattice/K-matrix; the slot-lemma 4-divisibility indicator; the sign of Zolotarev's permutation x ↦ Ax.
why: A single table with proofs makes the ES₅ sign transportable to every listed field, so that a theorem in any of them is immediately an ES₅ statement.
first_step: Write the one-page dictionary with proofs (each equality is short: the discriminant form is A/p in all cases) and check it numerically on all words for p < 10⁴.

title: Track full Zaremba as ES's closest structural analogue
connection: Zaremba (bounded partial quotients for every q) is at density one (BK, Huang A=5) but not every q, like ES. Any 'every q' progress for some A (or for structured q like Niederreiter's prime powers) would show what kind of argument crosses that wall.
why: Shared obstruction profile: thin semigroup, polylog-to-power main terms, density-one results.
first_step: Search for post-2020 Zaremba results ('Zaremba conjecture every denominator', Kan, Frolenkov, Shkredov, 2023–2026) and record whether any is 'every q' for some A.

title: Profinite Furstenberg: closed ×k-invariant subsets of Ẑ and the ES-hard set
connection: Furstenberg: every infinite closed ×2,×3-invariant subset of the circle is everything. ES certificate existence is closed under n → kn; the closure in Ẑ (or in the solenoid) of the 'certificate-free' set is invariant under division by units? Formulate the right dynamical system on Ẑ and classify its closed invariant sets.
why: Odd: a topological rigidity statement on Ẑ could say the profinite hard set is exactly the squares, which is the B1 picture.
first_step: Write down the action (ℤ_{>0}, ×) on Ẑ and determine which closed invariant subsets contain the profinite square-mimicking points.

title: Unipotent flows and ES words: the horocycle parametrisation of minus-continuants
connection: Margulis used unipotent orbits. The matrices M(t) = [[t, −1],[1, 0]] are products of a unipotent [[1, t],[0, 1]] and a fixed rotation, so ES words M(u)M(t)M(v) are points on products of horocycle segments. Read ES as a statement about a three-step 'unipotent walk' hitting a target integer matrix.
why: Puts ES words into the language of unipotent dynamics, where every-orbit statements exist.
first_step: Write M(u)M(t)M(v) = n(u) w n(t) w n(v) w and characterise which targets [[p, ·],[·,·]] are reachable with t ∈ 4ℤ; compare with horospherical equidistribution scales.

title: Egyptian fractions on topological groups (Ross): ES in the circle group or in Q_p
connection: Ross extends structure results on sets of Egyptian fractions to subsets of topological groups. An ES analogue in R/Z or Q_p asks which elements are 3-term sums from a discrete generating set.
why: Topological closures of the set of 3-term sums (accumulation points are 2-term sums, etc.) give a 'derived set' picture; ES points must avoid being only limit points.
first_step: Read arXiv:2410.24165 to see which structure theorems carry over and whether derived-set orders give constraints on 4/n.

title: Lens-space/Seifert covering maps as transport between ES(n) and ES(dn)
connection: A d-fold fibre-preserving cover of the Seifert space M(0; (x,1),(y,1),(z,1)) multiplies e(M) by a factor depending on how fibres unwrap; for unwrapping that keeps β_i = 1 one gets ES-type equations for other n.
why: If covers map ES(n') solutions to ES(n) solutions with n' | n or n | n', it is a topological composition law; combined with an inductive scheme it would give ES for products.
first_step: Work out Euler numbers of covers of Seifert spaces with three exceptional fibres (Jankins–Neumann formulas).

title: ES as an integer-programming feasibility problem: divisor enumeration per p; flatness ideas need a convex relaxation
connection: For fixed p, ES is the feasibility of a small polynomial system over Z; after fixing the Type (I/II) and parameters it reduces to divisor enumeration (factorization), so ES is easy per p in practice; Lenstra/Kannan (fixed-dimension LINEAR integer programming) do not directly apply to these quadratic constraints.
why: If a slice can be relaxed to a convex body whose integer points are solutions, Khinchine's flatness theorem (lattice width) could force a point — this needs a genuinely convex formulation, which the quadratic slices lack.
first_step: Formulate one Type II slice as a lattice-width question; compute the width for hard primes and see whether Khinchine's flatness bound could force a point.

title: Thick object: the multiplicative group (ℤ/pℤ)^× and its subgroup lattice
connection: ES certificates for p correspond to residues of p modulo many 4ad, but one could also look mod p: x ≡ ? mod p. The set {x : 4x ≡ … mod p} is 'thick' (size p); extraction rule: lift to ℤ with size constraints.
why: Generator-matrix item (thick object × extraction rule): (ℤ/p)^× as thick object with an archimedean extraction rule.
first_step: Write ES Type II as a condition on a residue mod p plus a size bound and check whether the residue set has structure (subgroup/coset).

title: Denominator ratios as slopes
connection: Parameterize y/z by a reduced rational slope and express the ES condition in terms of its numerator and denominator.
why: A rational slope organizes triples differently from fixing x and might reveal short covering families.
first_step: Derive the divisibility condition for y=ku,z=kv with gcd(u,v)=1.

title: Geometry of numbers in moving boxes
connection: Study certificate lattices with anisotropic boxes adapted to denominator size rather than symmetric balls.
why: The natural coordinates can have very different scales, affecting any useful volume estimate.
first_step: For a fixed auxiliary modulus, derive the lattice determinant and plot the feasible box as p varies.

title: Star–triangle arithmetic moves
connection: Test the electrical star–triangle transformation as a source of rational three-variable identities with controlled denominator factors.
why: The network equality is exact, but integer preservation needs explicit extra conditions.
first_step: Write the star–triangle formulas and solve their integrality requirements for small positive integer inputs.

title: Reciprocal convexity bounds
connection: Use convexity of 1/t to derive necessary bounds on denominator sums and imbalance within a chosen search region.
why: These bounds are elementary and can reduce search without risking false sufficiency claims.
first_step: Derive Jensen and tangent-line bounds for ordered x≤y≤z satisfying the reciprocal sum.

title: Harmonic–arithmetic mean constraints
connection: Relate denominator spread to the fixed reciprocal sum through mean inequalities.
why: Quantitative spread bounds can distinguish balanced and highly skewed certificate families.
first_step: Derive the sharp lower bound on x+y+z over positive real solutions and inspect the integer gap for small p.

title: Small-root lattice attacks on residual equations
connection: Check whether a chosen ES parametrization yields a modular polynomial with a genuinely small unknown suitable for lattice small-root methods.
why: Cryptanalytic techniques are relevant only when explicit size inequalities are met.
first_step: Derive one univariate modular residual and check whether a Coppersmith theorem covers its degree, modulus, and root bound.

title: Logarithmic geometry of denominator exclusions
connection: Treat denominator vanishing loci as a marked divisor and compare charts respecting that divisor.
why: A log-geometric description may organize which coordinate changes preserve the relevant open set.
first_step: Write the marked boundary for two birational charts and compute how each boundary factor transforms.

title: Lens space L(p,A) not homotopy-equivalent to L(p,1), bounding a 3-chain plumbing
connection: p/A = [[v,t,u]] means L(p,A) bounds the linear plumbing with Euler numbers −v,−t,−u. Whitehead: L(p,q) ≃ L(p,q′) iff qq′ ≡ ±m² (mod p). For p ≡ 1 (4) prime, (A/p) = −1 ⇔ L(p,A) ≄ L(p,1). So ES₅(p) ⇔ some lens space of order p that is not homotopy-equivalent to L(p,1) bounds a negative-definite linear plumbing with 3 vertices.
why: Turns ES₅ into a 3-manifold statement about the 'plumbing length' of homotopy types, where the homotopy type is the ES sign.
first_step: Tabulate min plumbing length over the non-L(p,1) homotopy class for p < 10⁵ (= λ(p)); look for 4-manifold invariants (d-invariants, Casson–Walker) that bound plumbing length from above.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0173] git grep -il 'lens' BRAINSTORM | head; read bsA_lens_homotopy_surgery.md; check whether Greene's lens space realisation (which lens spaces arise from integer surgery on knots in S³) applies to ES's family.

[free_opus-0422] Translate the repo's ES₅ CF-length-3 condition precisely into plumbing weights (−a₁, −a₂, −a₃) and check whether the congruence constraints correspond to a natural topological property (e.g. spin structure, lattice embedding).
refs: Greene, 'The lens space realization problem' (Ann. Math 2013)

title: Möbius inversion on the divisor lattice (Rota) for the certificate indicator: express 1[∃ a | N, a ≡ −1 (m)] via Möbius function of the lattice of divisors
connection: The event 'some divisor lies in a class' is a union over divisors; inclusion–exclusion on the divisor lattice gives an exact alternating formula; the 'Möbius algebra' of the divisor poset might simplify when the class condition is a character condition.
why: Exact combinatorial formula alternative to the character-sum formula; may expose cancellation structure.
first_step: Write the formula for N squarefree with ω factors (2^ω terms) and compare its complexity to the character formula (φ(m) terms); use whichever is smaller per regime.
refs: Rota, 'On the foundations of combinatorial theory I'

title: Unit-fraction Tilings: Egyptian squares (Rédei-style tiling by rectangles of area 1/n)
connection: Tiling a rectangle by rectangles of sides 1/a×1/b relates to Egyptian decompositions ↔ ES as a 3-piece tiling of a 4×p-ish rectangle.
why: Tilings give geometric invariants (Dehn-type) that sometimes prove impossibility or existence.
first_step: Formulate: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ tiling of a (4·lcm)-strip; check if any Dehn-like invariant is non-trivial.

title: Lattice reduction geometry: ES as short vector in a p-dependent lattice of bounded dimension
connection: Repo has lattices L_ρ; Minkowski's theorem gives short vectors pointwise ↔ need vector in a prescribed coset/positive cone.
why: Minkowski is pointwise (T-type size squeeze); the question is whether some lattice of determinant ≍ p has a short vector that is automatically a certificate.
first_step: List repo lattice forms; for each compute Minkowski's guaranteed short vector length vs certificate size bound.

title: Coppersmith small-root method: find (d, d′) with dd′ = 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C as a small root of a bivariate polynomial
connection: Writing d = 4Ck − 1 makes the condition (4Ck−1)·d′ = 4Cp+1, a bivariate polynomial with a small root (k, d′). Coppersmith/Howgrave-Graham finds small roots when they exist below a size bound.
why: This is the crypto-native 'factoring with a hint' toolbox. A lattice whose reduced basis has a short vector exactly when a certificate exists would be an existence criterion of a new kind (a Minkowski bound).
first_step: Set up f(C,k) = 4uCk − u − k − p and compute the Coppersmith bound X·Y ≤ p^δ for which small roots are guaranteed to be found; compare with expected certificate sizes (C,k ≤ ?).
alt_first_steps: [translate-0075] Build the Howgrave-Graham lattice for fixed small C and p ~ 10¹²; check whether the reduced-basis norm predicts certificate existence (compare with ground truth).
[signature-0140] Express the ES fixed-C divisor condition as a polynomial congruence and test Coppersmith bounds on p up to a small bit size, comparing against direct divisor enumeration.
refs: unverified: Coppersmith, Small solutions to polynomial equations, and low exponent RSA vulnerabilities (1996)

title: Learning-with-errors / lattice duality analogy: no
connection: LWE hardness vs ES certificate search ↔ superficial: both involve modular linear relations.
why: Probably vacuous; kept low confidence as a pointer that lattice duality (transference) could convert 'no certificate' into 'short dual vector' — a dual certificate of failure.
first_step: Formulate: if no certificate in lattice coset, transference gives a short dual vector; compute dual vectors for (★)-failing p = 409 and see if they look structured.

title: Bianchi-group hyperbolic counting for the Gaussian sibling ES_Q1
connection: ES_Q1 over ℤ[i] Type II analogues are SL₂(ℤ[i]) matrices; lattice counting in hyperbolic 3-space for Bianchi groups has spectral asymptotics.
why: A sibling with its own automorphic theory where failures (2+5i, …) exist — testing whether spectral main terms predict them.
first_step: Write the ES_Q1 Type II analogue as a Bianchi lattice-count and compare predicted counts at failing Gaussian primes.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0342] For the six ES_Q1 failures (2+5i, 4+5i, …), compute their position relative to Bianchi group fundamental domain features (cusps, elliptic points).
refs: Elstrodt–Grunewald–Mennicke, Groups Acting on Hyperbolic Space (1998)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Triangles with integer altitudes and inradius n/4 (the x > n/2 subfamily)
connection: 1/h_a + 1/h_b + 1/h_c = 1/r. A triangle with altitudes x,y,z exists iff the reciprocals satisfy the triangle inequality, i.e. iff x > n/2 for the smallest x. So 'ES with x ∈ (n/2, 3n/4]' ⇔ a triangle with integer altitudes and inradius n/4.
why: It is a natural geometric sub-variant. It turns out to be false at every prime p ≡ 1 (4) (see first step), which is a clean calibration: the triangle inequality on reciprocals is incompatible with ES at hard primes.
first_step: DONE (cheap test, scripts/z52b_translate_cheap.py): the variant FAILS for EVERY prime p ≡ 1 (4) (checked < 1500 after a reviewer caught an ordering bug in the first script; proof: if all of x,y,z > p/2 then x,y < p, so z = kp with 4k ≡ 1 (mod p) and k ≤ (p+1)/4, impossible for p ≡ 1 (4)). So the integer-altitude strengthening is false at all hard primes; record it as a dead variant.
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0352] For p ≤ 10⁴, classify ES solutions by whether 1/x < 1/y + 1/z holds (altitude-realisable) and check if every p has a realisable one.
[signature-0055] For hard primes ≤ 10⁵, compute the fraction of ES solutions satisfying the triangle inequality on (1/x,1/y,1/z); look up 'triangles with integer altitudes' parametrisations.
[signature-0340] Derive the altitude/inradius identity under rational side-area normalization and check which integral triangle families yield denominators matching 4/n.
[signature-0356] Homogenize the triangle identity and ES surface side by side and identify whether either has a birational map preserving positive rational points.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Categorification: R(p) as dim H⁰ of a complex whose Euler characteristic is explicit
connection: If certificates span H⁰ of a natural complex (e.g. Koszul complex of the divisibility conditions) with χ = explicit positive quantity and H¹ small, existence follows ↔ Euler-characteristic arguments in algebraic combinatorics.
why: Speculative but concrete: Euler characteristics are exact and often computable from local data — an R-type input.
first_step: Write the Koszul complex for the ideal (4uC − 1)·k − (p + u) over a polynomial ring truncated by degree bounds and compute its Euler characteristic numerically for small p.

title: Ehrhart / lattice points on dilated segments: N(p; u,B) as an Ehrhart quasi-polynomial value
connection: The denumerant N(n; u,B) counts lattice points on the segment {ux + By = n, x,y ≥ 0} — a rational polytope; its Ehrhart quasi-polynomial has period uB ↔ ES(★) ⟺ for some (u,B), the quasi-polynomial at n = p hits the 'minimal' constituent.
why: Ehrhart reciprocity relates N(n) and N(−n − u − B) (interior points); p = 4CuB − u − B means −p − u − B = −4CuB: the Ehrhart reciprocity partner of p is a multiple of uB — a crisp algebraic restatement of the (★) condition.
first_step: Verify via Ehrhart–Macdonald reciprocity: N(p) relates to the interior count at 4CuB; derive (★) ⟺ 'p's reciprocity partner is divisible by 4uB' and check numerically.

title: Rigidity reading: 3 cone points (triangle groups) are rigid, 4 cone points have moduli — mirrors 3-term ES hard vs 4-term easy
connection: Teichmüller space of S²(x₁,…,x_k) has dimension 2k − 6: zero for triangle groups, positive for 4 or more cone points ↔ ES with 3 terms is hard while the 4-term analogue is easy.
why: A heuristic link between geometric rigidity and arithmetic sparsity (polylog solutions). It suggests looking for 'deformation' arguments that start from a 4-cone-point solution (always available) and degenerate a cone point (order → ∞ or merging) to reach 3 points.
first_step: Write the degeneration: 4/p = 1/a + 1/b + 1/c + 1/d with d → merging (1/c + 1/d = 1/e) — count how often a 4-term solution has two terms merging to a unit fraction (same as batch A's 4→3 collapse item; check the geometric version gives anything new).

title: Polyhedral/tiling vertex equations as Egyptian equations: classification precedents
connection: Vertex-configuration equations of tilings (e.g. Σ 1/k_i = const for polygons meeting at a vertex) are Egyptian-fraction equations solved by finite enumeration ↔ ES is the same algebra with an n-dependent right side.
why: Shows ES as 'a tiling-vertex equation at curvature 4/n'; mostly orientation, but hyperbolic tiling enumeration software could enumerate ES-type configurations quickly.
first_step: Write the angle condition for three regular polygons at a vertex of a hyperbolic tiling with prescribed angle defect and relate to 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/n.

title: Guth–Katz polynomial partitioning for real ES solution geometry
connection: Polynomial partitioning bounds incidences in ℝ^d; ES solutions are lattice points on the real cubic surface 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx).
why: Upper bounds on lattice points near the surface across many n bound pair correlations of f(n).
first_step: Bound #{(n, x,y,z) : n ≤ N} incidences with the one-parameter family of surfaces via partitioning and compare with known Σ f(n)² ≍ N log^? estimates.
refs: Guth–Katz, On the Erdős distinct distances problem in the plane, Ann. Math. 181 (2015)

title: Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira joint equidistribution of integer points and their orthogonal lattices
connection: AES prove joint equidistribution of primitive integer points on spheres together with the shape of their orthogonal lattice; ES certificates carry both a 'point' (solution) and an associated lattice (L_ρ).
why: Joint equidistribution could say the ES-relevant lattice shape is generic, so short vectors in cones (ES) exist for most representations.
first_step: Formulate the ES lattice L_ρ at p as the orthogonal lattice of a vector and check whether AES's setup matches.
refs: Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira, Integer points on spheres and their orthogonal grids, arXiv:1411.1272
Aka–Einsiedler–Shapira, Integer points and their orthogonal lattices, arXiv:1502.04209

title: Rademacher symbol (conjugacy-invariant) = linking number of the modular knot with the trefoil (Ghys)
connection: Ghys: for hyperbolic γ ∈ SL₂(ℤ), the Rademacher symbol (the conjugacy-invariant version of Rademacher's function Φ, differing by a sign/trace correction) equals the linking number of the closed geodesic (modular knot) in SL₂(ℝ)/SL₂(ℤ) = S³ − trefoil with the trefoil. If the ES sign is a function of Φ(γ_w), it becomes a linking number.
why: A topological meaning for the sign would bring knot-theoretic positivity/counting (Ghys's theorem) to ES; at least it is an exact dictionary.
first_step: Compute Φ(γ_w) for words (from the cutting sequence) and test whether Φ mod 4 determines the slot-lemma sign.
alt_first_steps: [tools-0165] Compute Rademacher symbols Ψ(M) for ES₅ certificate matrices at many p and look for a forced value range.
refs: Ghys, Knots and dynamics, Proc. ICM 2006

title: Browning–Vinogradov effective Ratner for SL(2,ℝ)⋉ℝ² (gaps in √n mod 1) for affine ES lattices
connection: Browning–Vinogradov make Ratner equidistribution effective on ASL(2) to count affine-lattice events; ES Type I/II with a fixed shift (p) are affine-lattice problems (L + p·v).
why: Affine lattices capture the inhomogeneous p-dependence that homogeneous equidistribution misses.
first_step: Formulate the ES certificate set as points of an affine lattice in a region and check the BV setup.
refs: Browning–Vinogradov, Effective Ratner theorem for SL(2,R)⋉R^2 and gaps in √n modulo 1, J. LMS 94 (2016), arXiv:1311.6387

title: Toric surface with three boundary curves: HJ-length-3 cones as compact toric surface data
connection: A 2-dim cone of type 1/p(1,A) whose resolution has 3 rays corresponds to a toric surface patch. ES₅ asks for a smooth fan refinement with 3 new rays whose self-intersections (−v,−t,−u) give p, with a twist class.
why: Toric geometry turns the condition into lattice-polygon combinatorics (Oda's 12/24 theorem for complete fans), which might give global constraints linking different A's.
first_step: Write the 3-ray refinement condition as a lattice-polygon statement; check whether completing the fan to a compact toric surface forces relations between v, t, u and A (mod 4).
refs: Oda, Convex bodies and algebraic geometry (1988)

title: Hidden Number Problem formulation: recover/obtain A from partial information on A·x mod p
connection: Boneh–Venkatesan's HNP finds α from approximations of α·t_i mod p. The ES₅ condition r(p/A) = 3 says A/p lies near 1/v with a prescribed error structure (A = (p+u)/v), an approximation statement about A mod p.
why: HNP and lattice-reduction tools are native for 'find an element mod p with given approximate multiples'. Reversing them (choose A with small multiples) is a geometry-of-numbers existence question.
first_step: Write the ES₅ word condition as 'vA ≡ u (mod p) with uv small, (u,v) in a hyperbolic region'; check the Minkowski bound for the lattice {(x, y) : y ≡ Ax mod p} restricted to non-residue A.

title: Lefschetz number of a map on a 'certificate space' with ES-certificate fixed points
connection: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem: L(f) ≠ 0 ⇒ fixed point. A continuous or algebraic self-map of a compact space whose fixed points are ES certificates and whose Lefschetz number is computable would prove existence.
why: It is the classic topological existence engine; the windmill is its discrete special case. A finite-field version (Lefschetz trace for Frobenius) counts points over F_q, not integral points.
first_step: Record the attempts in invol_topological.md; look for algebraic maps on U_n's compactification whose fixed loci are positive points (e.g. the cyclic permutation composed with a birational involution).

title: Arithmetic topology (Morishita): Legendre symbol as mod-2 linking number of prime knots
connection: In arithmetic topology (q/p) is the mod-2 linking number of 'prime knots' p and q in Spec ℤ. (A/p) = Σ_q v_q(A) lk(p,q) mod 2, and Rédei symbols are Milnor triple-linking numbers. ES₅ asks p to link oddly with the 'certificate link' of some word.
why: The dictionary might suggest topological constructions (Seifert surfaces = genus-theory objects) that force an odd linking. Speculative, but categorically sound.
first_step: Read Morishita, Knots and Primes ch. 4–8; translate the slot lemma into linking-number language and see whether a Seifert-surface argument suggests a certificate.

title: Quasi-Monte Carlo: rank-1 lattice rules with generator A and HJ length 3 as 'worst' lattices
connection: A 2-D rank-1 lattice rule {(k/p, kA/p)} has quality governed by the partial quotients of A/p (Zaremba index; Niederreiter). HJ length 3 with huge digits means a very bad lattice rule. ES₅ asks for a bad lattice rule with a QNR generator.
why: QMC has existence theorems for good lattice rules for all p (Korobov) and explicit constructions for prime powers (Niederreiter). The extremal-bad side with a character condition is a dual question.
first_step: Formulate ES₅ in QMC terms: ∃ QNR A such that the lattice rule has a lattice point (v, u) with uv small and vA − u = p (the dual lattice has a very short vector). Compare with Korobov averaging over A ∈ QNR.
refs: Niederreiter, Random Number Generation and Quasi-Monte Carlo Methods (1992)

title: Toric log del Pezzo / weighted projective planes from Egyptian triples (Nill–Kasprzyk dictionary)
connection: Unit-fraction equations classify reflexive/Gorenstein toric Fano simplices (1 = Σ 1/k_i ↔ weighted projective spaces P(q₀,…) with q_i | Σq). For ES, the weights (yz, xz, xy)/g give a weighted P² whose 'index' (Σq)/lcm(q) is tied to 4/n. ES ⇔ some weighted P² has a prescribed index-type invariant.
why: The toric-Fano classification literature (Kasprzyk, Nill, Conrads) has tools for exactly 'which weight vectors satisfy divisibility conditions'. That gives a geometric home for the original Egyptian equation.
first_step: Work out the exact invariant: for P(a,b,c) with (a,b,c) ∝ (1/x,1/y,1/z), compute (a+b+c)/lcm(a,b,c) and the Gorenstein index in terms of n; check against Kasprzyk's tables of fake weighted planes.
refs: Conrads, Weighted projective spaces and reflexive simplices (2002)
Kasprzyk, Bounds on fake weighted projective space (2009; check)

title: Small vector + congruence ⇒ equality, for the cubic ES polynomial (Ankeny-style)
connection: Thue/Ankeny: if F(v) ≡ 0 mod M and |F(v)| < M then F(v) = 0. For F = 4xyz − p(xy+yz+zx) with |v| ≈ X: |F| ≈ pX² and Minkowski gives |v| ≈ M^{1/3}; the scales match when M ≳ p³, X ≈ p.
why: The scale bookkeeping does not immediately fail; the open question is whether an affine sublattice of index ~M on which F ≡ 0 (mod M) exists.
first_step: Classify affine sublattices of ℤ³ on which F vanishes mod q for primes q (e.g. the Type II slices y,z ≡ 0 mod p); see if CRT combinations of such slices reach M ≳ p³.

title: Conjecture I3 as ES's cleanest 'universality' cousin of Cauchy/Waring
connection: Cauchy's polygonal theorem and Waring are universality statements. Conjecture I3 (FRONTIER §7: every n > 2 433 600 is tuv − u − v with t, u, v ≥ 3) is a sign-free, prime-free universality statement for a cubic polynomial; universality proofs for polynomials (Cauchy's lemma, Linnik's 7 cubes via ternary forms) are natural models.
why: I3 drops ES's 4ℤ constraint on t; a proof technique for I3 is the right first test of any universality mechanism.
first_step: Read EXSET_I3.md / I3_DEEP_ASTRA.md; then try a Cauchy-lemma-style reduction: for fixed t, tuv − u − v = n ⟺ (tu − 1)(tv − 1) = tn + 1 — ask which t make 'tn + 1 has a factorisation into two factors ≡ −1 (mod t), both ≥ 3t − 1' provable for all large n.
refs: Nathanson, Proc. AMS 99 (1987) 22-24 (A short proof of Cauchy's polygonal number theorem)

title: Erdős–Graham coloring methods
connection: Ask whether techniques around the Erdős–Graham Egyptian-fraction problem suggest a useful partition of denominator candidates.
why: Coloring or density arguments might inspire family selection even if their conclusions involve many terms.
first_step: Locate a verified statement and proof source, then check whether any intermediate lemma controls a fixed small number of terms.

title: Sylvester-style product recurrences
connection: Check how classical product recurrences for Egyptian fractions encode divisibility, then ask whether alternative initial conditions yield three-term terminal states.
why: Product recurrences provide exact rational identities whose length and congruences can be tracked.
first_step: Locate a reliable source for the recurrence, derive it independently, and test modified initial parameters symbolically.

title: Post the single-integer lower tail as a MathOverflow question
connection: FRONTIER §2's reduction ('a specific integer tied to p must have a divisor in a class with modulus part of the solution') is a clean, citable question for MO: 'Is there any known theorem giving ≥1 divisor in a tied residue class for every n?'
why: MO has answered 'is there any theorem of shape X' questions well (experts recall obscure results); low cost.
first_step: Write the MO question with the precise statement (4Cp+1 has a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C for some C), the heuristic count log²p, and the known results (Lenstra upper bound, almost-all results); post under number-theory tag.

title: Erdős's 'covering congruences' letters and the Erdős–Selfridge sign heuristics as hints for which modulus families to try
connection: Erdős proposed many covering-type conjectures; his letters to Selfridge (published partially) contain rules of thumb for when covering fails; a historian's reading may give the exact reason Erdős believed ES was 'not provable by congruences alone'.
why: History-of-ideas item; cheap.
first_step: Search 'Erdős Straus conjecture congruences cannot suffice Erdős remark' and read Erdős–Graham 'Old and new problems' §on unit fractions for Erdős's own assessment.
refs: Erdős–Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980)

title: Category-theoretic / functorial view: ES as a natural transformation between the functors n ↦ Div(4Cn+1) and n ↦ residue classes
connection: Half-joke, half-meta: which constructions are *natural in n*? Polynomial identities are natural transformations ℤ[n] → solutions; Mordell–Schinzel says no natural transformation exists on square classes. The question becomes: what is the weakest 'naturality' (e.g. natural in the category of ℤ with Legendre-symbol decorations) that admits a solution map?
why: Organises the 'what kind of identity' question by the structure the identity is allowed to see (polynomial / Legendre symbols / factorisation of 4Cn+1 / full factorisation of n). A hierarchy of 'identity types' with the known no-go results placed on it is a useful map.
first_step: Write the hierarchy: (0) polynomial in n; (1) polynomial in n and ⌊√n⌋; (2) depending on n mod M for bounded M (= covering); (3) depending on Legendre symbols of n w.r.t. bounded primes; (4) depending on the factorisation of 4Cn+1 for bounded C; (5) unbounded. Place Mordell–Schinzel at (0), and ask which level ES's known data refutes.

title: Community: write up the C-form exceptional primes + QNR lemma as a short arXiv note / MO question to invite elementary explanations
connection: The observations (C-form strictly weaker than ES; four exceptional primes below 20000 with no certificate to C = 60000; every certificate divisor is a QNR mod p) are elementary and crisp — ideal for an MO question 'Why does 409 have no factorisation 4C·409 + 1 = ab with a ≡ b ≡ −1 mod 4C?'
why: Crowd-sourced elementary number theory is strong at exactly this kind of question; a quick answer would either kill a sub-conjecture (local obstruction) or reveal a mechanism.
first_step: Verify the four exceptions independently (Pari), extend to 10⁶ for the list, then post on MO with the QNR lemma.

title: Mordell's identities ↔ Rosati/Yamamoto/Aigner tables as an early 'covering system' history
connection: Mordell's mod-840 reduction and later moduli (Yamamoto, Salez's modular filters) form an increasing covering chain ↔ covering-system theory (Erdős, Hough's minimum modulus theorem).
why: Hough proved covering systems with distinct moduli have bounded minimum modulus; ES coverings are of a different type (non-distinct, polynomial classes), and stating precisely why Hough's method doesn't apply is cheap.
first_step: Write the ES modular filters as a 'polynomial covering' and check whether Hough/Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method covers polynomial-residue coverings.
refs: R. Hough, Ann. of Math. 181 (2015) — check citation

title: Erdős–Graham book 'Old and new problems' chapter on unit fractions as a map of solved/unsolved
connection: Erdős–Graham (1980) list dozens of unit-fraction problems; several since solved (Croot, Bloom, Martin) ↔ ES.
why: Each solved neighbour gives a method; an indexed table 'problem → method → why it fails for ES' extends the z52 dossier cheaply.
first_step: Pull every unit-fraction problem from erdosproblems.com with status 'proved' and record the key method in one line each.

title: Meta: 'what would a counterexample look like' dossier
connection: A counterexample p would be a non-BM integral Hasse failure with R(p) = 0 and all slices failing ↔ list necessary properties (mod 840 square class, all F_q lines fail, sterile-point local behaviour, …).
why: Necessary-condition dossiers guide disproof searches and reveal if the conditions become contradictory.
first_step: Collect all PROVED necessary conditions for an ES counterexample from repo into one list; compute the density of primes satisfying them simultaneously.

title: Natural-proofs-style meta-barrier for ES
connection: Razborov–Rudich formalise why 'natural' combinatorial properties can't prove circuit lower bounds; the campaign's barrier theorems (B1–B9) are informal analogues for ES proof strategies.
why: A formal meta-barrier would classify proof strategies by a property (e.g. 'treats the p-tied integer as random') and prove they can't succeed against a pseudorandom model where ES fails.
first_step: Construct a random model (consistent with all known local and average facts) in which ES fails for a positive proportion of p, and list which proof techniques are 'relativising' to it.

title: Explicit inequalities + finite check as the complete proof shape
connection: Bertrand's postulate is fully proved by an explicit inequality for n ≥ n₀ plus a hand check. For ES, collect every inequality-type sufficient condition (e.g. M_BM(p) > |X(p)| bound, Lagrange-pigeonhole ratio > 1 for some e, single-prime certificate count ≥ 1) and see if any admits an explicit lower-bound/upper-bound argument for all p ≥ p₀ with p₀ ≤ 10¹⁸.
why: Forces each mechanism to be phrased as an inequality between explicit quantities — useful even if none closes.
first_step: Write the 5 most promising sufficient conditions as explicit inequalities and evaluate both sides numerically at p ~ 10¹⁸ for the adversarial primes.

title: ES is a Π₁ sentence: bounded search, so independence from PA would imply truth
connection: With x ≤ y ≤ z, x ≤ 3n/4 and z ≤ n²-ish bounds (explicit poly(n)), ES is ∀n ∃(bounded) — Π⁰₁. Any counterexample is a standard integer; models of PA where ES fails contain a nonstandard counterexample.
why: Places ES alongside Goldbach-type statements; reverse-math/proof-theoretic analysis can say which fragments (IΔ₀ + exp?) could prove it.
first_step: Write down the explicit bound making ES a bounded-quantifier statement and note its consequence (any proof exists in a sufficiently strong theory iff true and provable).
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0192] Write the explicit bound on z in terms of n (from 1/z ≥ 4/n − 2/y …) and record the Π₁ form; check BRAINSTORM/logic_* memos for prior discussion.
[dividing-0287] Literature check: 'Π1 sentences number theory independence natural' (Friedman's work) — is any Diophantine-existence-for-all-n statement known independent?
[signature-0070] Write a minimal Turing machine (or Lean decidable predicate) that halts iff ES fails; compare its size with the bbchallenge Goldbach machines.
[translate-0133] Write the precise bounds (Curtiss/ET) and state ES as a Π⁰₁ formula; check whether 'almost all n' (Vaughan) is formalisable in IΣ₁.

title: Nonstandard analysis: an ES counterexample would be a 'nonstandard prime' with no standard certificate — apply the transfer principle to the almost-all results
connection: In a nonstandard model, Vaughan's exceptional-set bound says exceptional primes are 'rare'; Loeb-measure arguments sometimes convert density statements into structural statements about all elements of a 'generic' nonstandard set (as in Jin's sumset theorems).
why: Jin used nonstandard methods to prove sumset structure results that were hard classically; the ES analogue would be a structure theorem for the (hypothetical) exceptional set. Low confidence.
first_step: Formulate the hyperfinite failure object and see whether a known ergodic-theoretic theorem (via a correspondence principle) contradicts it. Likely only density results, but record.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0158] Read Jin, 'Freiman's inverse problem with small doubling property' (Adv. Math 2007) for the method; think whether 'exceptional primes' can be shown to have a forbidden structure.
[analogues-0209] Low priority; note.
refs: R. Jin, nonstandard methods in additive combinatorics

title: Proof complexity of bounded failures
connection: Compare lengths of machine-checkable unsatisfiability proofs for different bounded ES encodings.
why: Short proofs may reveal elementary exclusions worth expressing as human lemmas.
first_step: For several deliberately too-small boxes, compare proof sizes under direct and factorized encodings.

title: Trusted-kernel pipelines
connection: Route heuristic discoveries into a tiny theorem-checking kernel rather than trusting the search or symbolic algebra package.
why: The proof obligation stays explicit even when discovery uses complicated tools.
first_step: Choose one elementary family and separate its discovery script from a minimal proof of the resulting identity and divisibility conditions.

title: Total-search complexity questions
connection: Ask what complexity classification would follow if ES witnesses had a specified polynomial bit-length bound.
why: The conditional formulation separates existence from efficient verification and avoids assuming ES is already a total search theorem.
first_step: Write the witness relation and identify exactly which unproved size and existence statements are needed for a TFNP-style classification.

title: Parameterized complexity by factor count
connection: Treat the number of distinct auxiliary prime factors or modulus structure as an algorithmic parameter.
why: Subset-product search may be tractable in a parameter even when the integer itself is large.
first_step: Derive running-time bounds for residue selection in terms of factor count and group invariant factors.

title: Lean formalization of one family
connection: Formalize one elementary rational identity together with its positivity and divisibility hypotheses.
why: A small verified example establishes the shape of proof obligations without trying to formalize the whole campaign.
first_step: Choose the simplest directly checked family and locate the Lean lemmas needed for rational field simplification.

title: Integer–rational coercion discipline
connection: Treat exact division as a separate proved step before moving a parametrization from integers to rational identities.
why: This prevents silent truncation or unjustified integrality in machine and human proofs.
first_step: Write a typed proof outline for one formula, marking every use of integer divisibility and rational coercion.

title: A library of divisibility transport lemmas
connection: Collect reusable lemmas carrying divisibility through substitutions, gcd cancellation, and complementary factors.
why: These small facts recur across many distinct constructions and can reduce proof friction.
first_step: Formalize or precisely state five transport lemmas needed by the residual factor-pair equivalence.

title: Certified completeness of finite enumeration
connection: Prove the ordered-denominator bounds used by an exhaustive verifier and connect them to its loop limits.
why: A witness checker proves individual successes; a completeness proof also validates bounded absence claims.
first_step: Write a proof outline linking x and y inequalities to each loop endpoint of a toy exhaustive search.

title: Extracting certificate algorithms from proofs
connection: Given a constructive family theorem, extract the parameter-to-denominator function with its domain test.
why: The extracted algorithm connects proof structure to measurable search behavior.
first_step: Take one hand-proved family and write its domain predicate and witness constructor as separate pure functions.

title: Resultants as specialization filters
connection: Use resultants to detect when specialized auxiliary factors acquire common divisors or lose coprimality.
why: The resultant supplies an explicit finite arithmetic obstruction to naive factor independence.
first_step: Compute the resultant of two polynomial denominator factors and derive which primes can divide both specializations.

title: Mahler equations for recursive selectors
connection: Check whether a digit-recursive certificate selector has a generating function satisfying a functional equation involving z and z^b.
why: A functional equation could certify a recursive pattern if the selector recursion is proved first.
first_step: For a toy digit-based family, derive the coefficient recursion and test the resulting Mahler-type equation formally.

title: TFNP classification: ES-SEARCH and the parity (PPA) / pigeonhole (PPP) classes
connection: Assuming ES, 'given n, output (x,y,z)' is a total search problem. A windmill/parity proof would put it in PPA, a pigeonhole proof in PPP, a potential/descent proof in PLS. Fermat two-squares (Zagier windmill) is the canonical PPA-type number-theoretic search.
why: Complexity theory gives a vocabulary for the kind of non-constructive argument a proof could use. Proving ES-SEARCH lies in some class by an explicit reduction is a proof of ES.
first_step: Write the WINDMILL.md reduction (weighted parity of solutions) as a PPA instance template; check whether any known PPA-complete problem (e.g. 'Leaf') has a natural ES-shaped instance.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0065] Try to express ES as 'a graph with an odd-degree vertex has another' (PPA): build a graph on near-solutions where degrees are determined locally; see if one known odd-degree vertex (e.g. the trivial 'degenerate' solution 4/n = 1/n + 1/n + 2/n?) forces another.

[free_opus-0173] Read 'TFNP and number theory' (Papadimitriou; Ban et al. on PPA and factoring; Sotiraki–Zampetakis–Zirdelis PPP) and try to place ES-search: is there a parity argument (PPA) or pigeonhole (PPP)?
refs: Papadimitriou, On the complexity of the parity argument (JCSS 1994)

title: Property testing: can one certify ES(p) with o(log p) queries to an oracle for the factorisation of 4Cp+1?
connection: Query complexity of the existence problem given a factorisation oracle: how many C must be queried in the worst case (empirically) before a winner is found? The query sequence design (adaptive vs non-adaptive) is the algorithmic skeleton of a proof.
why: Worst-case query counts over p ≤ 10⁸ calibrate the 'depth' of a proof (K queries ⇒ a K-case argument).
first_step: Record C_min(p) distribution (non-adaptive) and design an adaptive rule (choose next C based on factorisation of previous 4Cp+1); measure the max number of queries for p ≤ 10⁷.

title: Formal: state and prove in Lean the C-form ⟹ ES implication and the T1 obstruction (odd squares have no C-form certificate)
connection: Two small, self-contained theorems; T1's reciprocity proof is a good test of mathlib's Jacobi symbol API.
why: Produces citable formalised lemmas and might reveal a slicker proof of T1 (formalisation often does).
first_step: Write Lean statement: ∀ m odd, ¬∃ (Type II coprime solution) for 4/m²; prove via Jacobi symbol reciprocity in mathlib.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0236] Write the Lean statements; prove the C-form ⟹ solution direction (pure algebra); attempt T1 via `jacobiSym` lemmas.
[tools-0321] Write T1 in Lean 4 with Mathlib's Jacobi symbol API and formalise the coprime Type I/II definitions.
refs: Elsholtz–Tao, Counting the number of solutions to the Erdős–Straus equation on unit fractions, J. Aust. Math. Soc. 94 (2013)

title: Proof complexity: does ES for p ≤ N have short resolution/cutting-plane certificates?
connection: Each ES(p) has a polynomial-size certificate (x,y,z) ↔ 'ES for all p ≤ N' has a certificate of size N·polylog; the question is whether a uniform short proof exists — Π₁ statements and bounded arithmetic.
why: Bounded arithmetic (S¹₂, IΔ₀) characterisations: if ES were provable in IΔ₀+Ω₁, there would be polynomial-time witnessing — certificate finding in poly(log p) time. This turns a proof-theoretic question into an algorithmic one.
first_step: Read Buss witnessing theorem; formulate 'ES provable in S¹₂ ⟹ poly(log p)-time certificate algorithm'. Test: is there a heuristic poly(log p) algorithm for certificates (yes, try small C)? Is it provably correct?

title: Two-squares in PPA (Zagier windmill) ↔ ES in PPA? A search-problem formulation of windmills
connection: Finding x²+y² = p is in PPA via the Zagier involution (and is known poly-time via Cornacchia) ↔ ES windmill involutions would put ES-search in PPA.
why: If ES-search were PPA-hard or PPA-complete under a natural encoding, that would mean ES's proof must be a parity argument — direct guidance.
first_step: Check the literature on 'Fermat two squares' complexity class membership (e.g. Goldberg–?); attempt to write an ES windmill as a PPA instance (a graph of degree ≤ 2 with p-dependent vertices).

title: Termination analysis tools (ranking functions) applied to an ES search loop
connection: Software verification proves loop termination via ranking functions ↔ ES ⟺ 'for c := 1,2,… test certificate(p,c)' terminates for all p.
why: Automated termination provers (AProVE, Ultimate) fail on number theory, but the framing exposes what invariant is needed: a ranking function = a quantity decreasing until success.
first_step: Write the search loop in C and run a termination analyser to see what it asks for (expect failure; record the missing invariant).

title: Walnut theorem prover for automatic-sequence statements about ES menus
connection: Walnut (Shallit) decides first-order statements about automatic sequences ↔ menu-coverage statements are automatic.
why: Fast way to prove/disprove finite-menu coverings rigorously (although B1 says they fail on primes, Walnut can check for structured n like 4^s + k families).
first_step: Encode the repo's 4^s + k family proofs in Walnut (base 4 automatic) as a test, then try open 4^s + 297 or 15·2^s + 1 families.

title: Automated conjecture generation (Graffiti / TxGraffiti / Ramanujan Machine) on ES statistics
connection: Ramanujan Machine-style search for formulas ↔ conjecture identities for M(p), R(p) moments, minimal certificates.
why: Automated conjecturing may find unexpected exact relations (e.g. between R(p) and class numbers).
first_step: Feed (p, R(p), h(−4p), h(4p), ε_p, n₂(p), Ω(p±1), …) for p ≤ 10⁶ into a Graffiti-like inequality-conjecturer; inspect outputs.

title: AlphaProof/LLM-prover attempts on ES sub-lemmas (e.g. I3 for structured p families)
connection: AI provers now solve Erdős problems of 'abundance' shape ↔ ES sub-lemmas with explicit families (15·2^s+1, 4^s+297).
why: Open thin families are concrete, bounded-difficulty targets suitable for AI+Lean pipelines.
first_step: Formulate 'ES holds for all 15·2^s + 1' as a Lean statement and give it to an AI prover with repo's window technique as hints.

title: Lean: formalise the repo's thin-family proofs ((J)62–(J)80) as computer-checked theorems
connection: Thin families proved computer-assisted ↔ Lean `decide`/`norm_num` certificates.
why: Formal verification gives external-grade confidence and makes them citeable.
first_step: Start with 3·2^s + 1 family: encode window certificate structure in Lean; estimate effort.

title: Formal-conjectures repository: add precise ES-adjacent conjectures (I3_𝒞, F_q lines)
connection: DeepMind's formal-conjectures repo collects Lean statements of open problems ↔ repo's sharp conjectures.
why: Formal statements invite AI provers and disprovers; disprovers could find counterexamples to over-strong conjectures quickly.
first_step: Check if formal-conjectures has ErdosProblems/242; draft Lean statements for I3_𝒞 and F₁₁ as PR candidates (user approval).

title: Deterministic polynomial-time ES algorithm as a stronger target ('constructive ES')
connection: A polylog-time certificate search with a proof of termination is ES plus an algorithm. Randomised factoring-based searches succeed heuristically in polylog trials. Derandomisation theory (hitting sets for structured sets) is the native frame.
why: Hitting-set constructions for 'divisor-in-class' events are a computational-complexity lens: an explicit small set of levels C guaranteed to contain a working one is exactly a pointwise theorem.
first_step: Measure, for p ≤ 10⁹ (repo data), the smallest universal family of levels covering all tested p; compare with hitting-set size lower bounds from the Mordell–Schinzel obstruction (any finite family fails).
alt_first_steps: [free_opus-0384] Define the algorithm (order trials by modulus), run on 10⁶ random primes near 10^30 (using trial division on candidate divisors only), record max steps / log³p.

title: Benchmark: build an 'ES-hard' dataset for AI provers (statements of sub-lemmas with known answers)
connection: AI-for-math benchmarks ↔ ES sub-lemmas (thin families, slice criteria, T1) with ground truth.
why: Gives the AI community a test bed tied to ES; attracts tool-builders.
first_step: Collect 30 sub-statements (PROVED ones with proofs, CERTIFIED computations, open ones) in a uniform format.

title: Decision-tree lower bound: any certificate search querying 'm | p + u' needs ≥ … queries in the worst case
connection: Adversary arguments in query complexity ↔ B1 CRT evasion as an adversary strategy.
why: Formalises B1 as a query-complexity statement: any algorithm with a fixed query order needs unbounded queries (under Dickson); clarifies that the obstacle is order-independent.
first_step: Write the adversary argument formally under Hypothesis H and state the lower bound in terms of menu size.

title: AlphaProof / LLM provers on campaign lemmas
connection: AI provers (AlphaProof 2024; DeepSeek-Prover, Kimina, Aristotle) solve olympiad-level formal problems; the campaign has many small formal lemmas (sterility, forcing lines, GT1) that are olympiad-like.
why: Automating the verification of small PROVED items frees effort and might find counterexamples to mis-stated lemmas.
first_step: Extract 10 short PROVED lemmas from DISCOVERIES.md into Lean statements and run an available open prover on them.

title: Arakelov/height view: ES solutions have height ≤ n³-type bound, a Π⁰₁ statement
connection: Positive solutions satisfy x ≤ 3n/4, y ≤ n²-ish and z ≤ n⁴-ish (Curtiss-type bounds), so ES is a Π⁰₁ arithmetic sentence. Heights in Arakelov theory bound points; existence of small-height points is a Siegel-lemma question.
why: Siegel's lemma or geometry of numbers on the torsor might produce small points if a linear structure is present (e.g. Type II at fixed C is linear in some coordinates).
first_step: State precisely the height bounds for positive solutions. Check whether any linear sub-system at fixed (C,d) has a Siegel-lemma solution of the right size.

title: Quantum complexity: under the observed polylog level bound, ES-search would be in FBQP (Shor), so classical hardness would reduce to factoring
connection: Given ES with polylog levels (as observed), a certificate is found by factoring polylog many integers 4Cp+1, which takes polynomial time with Shor's algorithm. So ES-SEARCH ∈ FBQP under the empirical level bound, and classical difficulty reduces to factoring.
why: Complexity calibration: any proof that yields an efficient classical algorithm for certificates without factoring would be surprising. Proofs are therefore likely non-constructive, or constructive only modulo factoring.
first_step: State precisely: (polylog level bound) ⇒ ES-SEARCH ≤_P FACTORING. Check whether a reverse reduction (factoring ≤ ES-SEARCH) is plausible.

title: Measure of joint failure along a lacunary level sequence C ∈ {2^j}
connection: Linnik's key estimate is the small measure of α where Σ e(2^v α) is large. Analogue: the set of p failing (★) at every level C = 2^j, j ≤ J, should have density ≈ Π_j(1 − P_j); measure its correlation structure.
why: Lacunary levels give nearly independent constraints (moduli 2^{j+2} are nested though!) — quantifies how much independence nested moduli really give.
first_step: Compute failure indicators at C = 2^j for p ≤ 10⁸ and estimate joint failure probabilities versus the independent model.

title: Compactness/ultraproduct: a nonstandard ES-failing prime
connection: Tao's Sendov proof takes a sequence of counterexamples with degree → ∞ and analyses a limit object. ES: an ultraproduct of hypothetical failing primes p_k → ∞ is a nonstandard prime p* with no internal certificate; internal theorems (Thm 2.2: M_BM(p*) ≥ c log²p*) hold by Łoś. Seek a contradiction in the nonstandard model (e.g. via a Loeb-measure equidistribution statement).
why: Compactness turns 'all large p' into 'one nonstandard p', making limit-object arguments available.
first_step: Write down which standard theorems about p transfer (counts, character sums) and which 'external' statements (limits of normalised counts) could be proved by Loeb-measure arguments.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Median U(p)/log²p rises 1.33 → 1.54 from 10⁶ to 10⁷ (log³ growth)
connection: Window medians (p ≡ 1 (4)): 1.33 at 10⁶, 1.54 at 10⁷; minimum 0.61 (10⁶) and 0.88 (10⁷).
why: Consistent with ET's log³ average; the lower envelope also rises — supports 'every prime has ≫ log²p solutions' at least empirically.
first_step: Compare min_{window} U(p)/log³p across windows; if flat, the conjectural lower bound U(p) ≫ log³p / (something) is the right target.

title: QRT-style invariant curves
connection: Look for birational two-variable maps preserving an exact auxiliary curve and producing new rational certificates.
why: An invariant map could generate recurrent families if integrality and positivity are controlled.
first_step: For a quadratic slice, derive a root-switch map and compute a rational invariant or show none appears at low degree.

title: Flag-algebra / SDP certificates for density inequalities on ES residue menus
connection: Razborov's flag algebras prove density inequalities via SDP; finite residue-menu questions ('what fraction of classes mod M can a menu of shape X cover') are density optimisation problems.
why: SDP duality gives certified upper bounds on coverage — sharpening B1-type statements quantitatively.
first_step: Formulate menu coverage mod M as an LP/SDP and compute the dual bound for small menus.
refs: Razborov, Flag algebras, J. Symbolic Logic 72 (2007)

title: Auxiliary-prime skeleton of the three-squares proof applied to ES windows
connection: Gauss/Dirichlet: choose an auxiliary prime q with (−n/q) = 1, build a form of determinant 1 representing n, then use one class. ES windows: auxiliary prime q ≡ 3 (4), (q/p) = −1, K = (p+q)/4 (FORCED_WINDOW). Mirror each step: is there an object 'of determinant 1' built from (p,q) whose uniqueness forces −1 ∈ Rat_q(K)?
why: The auxiliary-prime step is already in the campaign; the missing 'uniqueness of the class' step is the one Gauss had and ES lacks.
first_step: Write the window certificate as a statement about a binary/ternary form built from (p, q, K) and compute its genus/class structure for small cases.
refs: Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Ch. IV

title: Chevalley–Warning for the window system modulo e with a forced trivial solution
connection: Chevalley–Warning gives a nontrivial zero when the number of zeros is ≡ 0 (mod char) and a trivial zero exists. For window e (prime), consider the system over F_e in variables (exponent choices) encoding Π q_i^{ε_i} ≡ −1 · (trivial adjustment); design it so ε = 0 is a solution and the degree condition holds, forcing a nonzero ε.
why: The classical algebraic route from 'many variables relative to degree' to existence; here variables = prime factors of N_e.
first_step: Write the system for e = 3, 7, 11 with k prime factors and compute degree vs variables; find k at which Chevalley–Warning applies.

title: Bethe-ansatz-like counting of ES solutions via a quantum many-body spectrum
connection: Solutions of 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z ↔ Bethe roots of a 3-particle system where total 'momentum' 4/n is shared; completeness of Bethe ansatz = existence of a root configuration.
why: Completeness theorems for Bethe ansatz are existence statements proved for every n (e.g. XXX chain for all lengths), by algebraic rigidity — one of the two mechanisms (R) the campaign identified as able to give pointwise results.
first_step: Search 'Bethe ansatz Egyptian fractions' and 'Bethe equations unit fractions'; otherwise try to write the Bethe equations of a 3-magnon sector of a chain of length n and compare with the unit-fraction structure.

title: Physics of Egyptian fractions: resistor networks (parallel resistances add reciprocally)
connection: Parallel resistors: 1/R = Σ 1/R_i ↔ ES: can resistance p/4 be made from three integer resistors in parallel.
why: Recasts ES in electrical-network language; series-parallel networks and their combinatorics (e.g. counting resistances achievable with n unit resistors) might suggest generalisations (network with 3 components + series).
first_step: Formulate 'p/4 Ω from three integer-Ω resistors in parallel' and a relaxation allowing one series connection; count solutions of the relaxation.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0008] Search 'integer resistors three parallel rational conductance' and 'Khan resistor network Egyptian fractions'; check whether any representation-theoretic argument (Farey/Stern–Brocot for series–parallel) gives three-term unit-fraction sums.
[signature-0341] Translate 4/n into a three-branch parallel network and enumerate series-parallel reductions to see whether known ES identities emerge.
refs: S. A. Khan, 'Farey sequences and resistor networks' (Proc. Indian Acad. Sci. 2012)

title: Quantum computing: Shor-like period finding gives a divisor in a residue class?
connection: Shor's algorithm finds the order of a mod N; ES needs a divisor of 4Cp+1 in class −1 mod 4C. Quantum algorithms can find divisors in prescribed classes (by factoring fully), so ES solutions are findable in poly(log p) quantum time *if they exist* — trivially. Non-trivial: is there a quantum 'witness' structure (e.g. a hidden subgroup) that exists for every p?
why: Framing the existence as a hidden-subgroup problem might reveal an algebraic structure (subgroup!) which is what proofs need; low confidence.
first_step: Write the e-slice condition as 'the function g(a,b) = ab⁻¹ mod e on the divisor lattice has −1 in its image' and check whether the image is ever a coset of a subgroup (computation for N ≤ 10⁶).

title: Fractional quantum Hall hierarchy: the chain matrix as a K-matrix and the ES sign as an anyon-theory class
connection: Haldane–Halperin hierarchy states have tridiagonal K-matrices whose filling is an HJ continued fraction. The anyon theory is the discriminant form of K on ℤ^r/Kℤ^r (here ℤ/p). ES₅(p) ⇔ a 3-level hierarchy state with det K = p whose ℤ/p anyon braiding form is in the non-square class.
why: Abelian Chern–Simons theory classifies anyon theories with ℤ/p fusion into two classes (by the Gauss sum and chiral central charge). Physics constraints such as Gauss–Milgram relate the class to the signature and to spin structure.
first_step: Write the topological spins θ_x = e^{πi x²A/p} for the fan K-matrix; compute the Gauss–Milgram sum (odd/fermionic version) and relate it to the slot lemma.
refs: Wen, Quantum Field Theory of Many-Body Systems ch. 7 (K-matrix)

title: Physics: renormalisation-group picture of the HJ ladder λ(p) ≤ L as depth of a hierarchical lattice
connection: Hierarchical (Berker/Migdal–Kadanoff) lattices are built by iterated substitution. Chain matrices of length L are hierarchical networks of depth L. 'Some depth-3 hierarchical network with τ = p has a non-square pairing' is ES₅. RG flow of the resistance under substitution is a Möbius (continued-fraction) map.
why: The RG viewpoint makes HJ length a 'number of RG steps', and statistical physics has fixed-point and universality tools for such flows (though arithmetic exactness is needed here).
first_step: Write the resistance RG map for the ladder and identify the HJ digits as couplings; check whether the sign is an RG invariant mod 2.

title: Ford's divisors-in-intervals H(x,y,2y) method for divisors in residue classes
connection: Ford (Annals 2008) determined the order of #{n ≤ x : n has a divisor in (y,2y]} with a (log)^{−δ}(loglog)^{−3/2} factor; ES needs a divisor in a residue class mod 4C, and the analogous 'has a divisor in class' count.
why: Ford's structure (anatomy, entropy of divisor sets) predicts the shape of the ES lower tail and its failure modes.
first_step: Formulate H_m(x) = #{n ≤ x : n has a divisor ≡ −1 mod m with d ≤ √n} and compute it for m = 4C, C ≤ 50, x = 10^8; compare with Ford-type heuristics.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0233] Check whether 'divisors in intervals and residue classes' has been treated (search Ford, Hall–Tenenbaum 'Divisors', congruence restrictions).
refs: Ford, The distribution of integers with a divisor in a given interval, Ann. Math. 168 (2008)

title: Transfer: Selberg–Delange / Landau for counting H-confined N_C
connection: Counts of integers composed of primes in a set of Dirichlet density δ follow Landau–Selberg–Delange ~ c x (log x)^{δ−1}.
why: Gives the precise heuristic per-C failure probability, the input of ES Poisson models.
first_step: Compute δ_C = |H_C|/φ(4C) maximal over subgroups H_C ∌ −1 (which is 1/2 when −1 ∉ index-2 subgroups) and derive the model.

title: nx(n): number of distinct first denominators
connection: nx(n) = #{x : some solution has this smallest denominator}: 1,2,2,1,3,3,4,3,4,3,6,2,… (not in OEIS); at primes correlates like U (ρ=−0.65 with L(1,χ_p)).
why: nx is the 'first-step branching' of the greedy tree; lower bounds on nx(p) are ES; it is the quantity a sieve over x controls.
first_step: Fit nx(p) vs log p (likely ≍ log p, not log²p) and check whether nx(p) ≥ 1 has a shorter proof form (one-shift divisibility).
